summary: This RFC proposes the Network Block Transfer protocol, NETBLT, for rapid bulk transfer of large amounts of data between computers. It is reliable and flow controlled, built for high throughput over many network types. It was replaced by RFC 998.

eli5.summary: Instead of one tiny package at a time, you ship a truck full of data and check it in big groups so the trip is faster.

questions: how does netblt flow control work
subtitle: A protocol for fast, reliable transfer of large data blocks over networks

tldr.problem: Traditional network protocols send data one packet at a time, which wastes time confirming each packet separately. Large file transfers over diverse networks needed a better approach.
tldr.mechanism: NETBLT groups data into large buffers and transfers each buffer as a sequence of packets. It uses rate control (burst transmission) instead of windowing, negotiated flow parameters, and timers to maintain reliability and high throughput while adapting to different network conditions.
tldr.outcome: The protocol provided high-performance bulk transfer and served as an experimental transport layer. It was later superseded by RFC 998 but influenced the thinking around performance-oriented protocol design.

today: RFC 969 is Historic. It was superseded by RFC 998 and represents experimental thinking on high-performance bulk transfer protocols from the 1980s.

sections.title: Overview of NETBLT
sections.content:
NETBLT (Network Block Transfer) is a transport-level protocol for rapid bulk data transfer between computers. It is reliable and flow-controlled, designed to achieve maximum throughput over a wide variety of networks.

Unlike protocols that interact per-packet, NETBLT works with large data aggregates called buffers. A client provides data in buffers; NETBLT breaks each buffer into packets and transmits them. After transmission, the receiver verifies all packets arrived. If packets are missing, it requests retransmission. Only after a buffer is completely received does the receiver notify the sender to proceed with the next buffer. This per-buffer interaction is far more efficient than per-packet interaction.
sections.eli5: You give NETBLT a bucket of data at a time. It breaks the bucket into packets, sends them, checks they all arrived, and tells you when it is ready for the next bucket.

sections.title: Buffers, Packets, and Flow Control
sections.content:
NETBLT is designed to handle arbitrarily large transfers (up to 232 bytes) by working with buffers. The sending and receiving NETBLTs negotiate the buffer size during connection setup based on limits provided by the clients. All buffers except the last must be the same size. Buffer sizes are in bytes only; clients handle the fragmentation.

Buffers are broken into DATA packets and a final LDATA packet per buffer. Unlike buffers, all DATA packets save the last in a buffer must be the same size, and packet size is negotiated too. Large packets improve performance but must avoid Internet fragmentation.

NETBLT uses a novel flow control method called rate control instead of traditional windowing. The sender transmits packets in bursts at negotiated intervals. For example, it might send 5 packets, pause for a fixed time, then send 5 more. The burst size and burst rate are negotiated after each buffer to adapt to observed performance. This approach delivers higher throughput than windowing while keeping receiver and gateway buffers from overflowing.
sections.eli5: The protocol splits data into buckets and packages. Everything adjusts to match the slowest router or computer: not too big a package, not so many at once, and pauses between groups to let the next computer catch up.

sections.title: Connection Setup and Reliability
sections.content:
A NETBLT connection has three stages: connection setup, data transfer, and connection close. Each stage is completed reliably.

Connection setup uses an OPEN packet from the active client and a RESPONSE packet from the passive client. These packets negotiate flow control parameters (packet size, buffer size, burst size, burst rate), the maximum number of concurrent buffers, whether DATA/LDATA packets are checksummed, and death-timeout values.

During data transfer, the receiver sends GO to signal readiness, the sender transmits the buffer's DATA and LDATA packets, and the receiver responds with OK (all packets received) or RESEND (list of missing packets). Timers ensure reliability: a data timer detects when LDATA is lost, and a control timer detects missing OK/GO/RESEND messages. Both ends use death timers and KEEPALIVE packets to detect connection failure.

Connection close occurs when the sender has received OK for the last buffer and sends a DONE packet. The receiver acknowledges by closing its half. A dally period allows for DONE retransmission if it was lost.
sections.eli5: Both sides say hello and agree on sizes and speeds. As data flows, the receiver says 'ready' and 'got it all' or lists what is missing. Timers watch for lost messages. Either side can say 'I am dead' if they stop hearing from the other.

sections.title: Multiple Buffering and Protocol Layers
sections.content:
To increase performance, NETBLT supports multiple buffering: several buffers can be transmitted concurrently. While the receiver processes previous buffers and checks for missing packets, the next buffer starts sending, keeping data flowing continuously. This is far more efficient than lock-step transmission where the sender waits after each buffer.

Each buffer is modeled as a finite state machine. Buffers move through states (receiving, sending, resending, received, sent) as the protocol progresses. Multiple buffers are simply multiple state machines executing concurrently.

NETBLT is implemented directly on top of the Internet Protocol (IP) and was assigned a temporary protocol number of 255 (pending finalization).
sections.eli5: While you are checking bucket 1, bucket 2 can start sending, so the stream never stops. Each bucket knows what state it is in.

sections.title: Parameter Negotiation and Timing
sections.content:
All flow control parameters (packet size, buffer size, burst size, burst rate) are negotiated during connection setup and renegotiated after each buffer transmission. The active (initiating) client proposes initial values; the passive client can only make them more restrictive, never less. After data transfer, the receiver suggests new burst size and rate, and the sender applies its own more-restrictive values.

Parameter estimation is crucial for performance. Packet sizes typically range from 128 bytes to 1-2 thousand bytes; 576 bytes is barely adequate. Buffers can be 100 kilobytes or more. Burst sizes are usually 5 to 10 packets. Burst rates of 60 to 100 milliseconds work well on local networks. Timer values must estimate round-trip delays and transfer times and are adapted continuously based on observed performance.
sections.eli5: At the start, both sides suggest sizes and speeds. After each bucket, they tune based on how the last one went. These numbers depend heavily on the machines and network used.

sections.title: Packet Types and Format
sections.content:
NETBLT defines packet types for connection (OPEN, RESPONSE, KEEPALIVE, DONE, QUIT, QUITACK, ABORT), data transfer (DATA, LDATA, NULL-ACK, CONTROL), and control. Every packet begins with a standard header (local port, foreign port, checksum, version, packet type, packet length) and a 2-byte checksum.

OPEN and RESPONSE packets carry a connection unique ID, buffer size, transfer size, data segment size, burst parameters, death timeout, transfer mode (send or receive), maximum concurrent buffers, checksum flag, and optional client-specific data. CONTROL packets can contain multiple control messages (GO, OK, or RESEND), each with its own sequence number. DATA and LDATA packets include the buffer number, highest consecutive sequence received, packet number within the buffer, and data.
sections.eli5: Each packet type carries the right information for its job: setup packets agree on sizes; data packets carry the data and track which one is which; control packets confirm or request missing data.
